extracted.intended_audience: science communicators, university press officers, journalists, and researchers studying media coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Determinants and criteria that make scientific press releases likelier to be picked up by news media; useful for press officers, communication researchers, and authors crafting or evaluating press releases for news impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing a press release / press conference (presence as primary driver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing a press release. Press releases or press conferences were the initial source of ideas for 40-50% of news stories, and 45% of health news stories did not go beyond a news release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as the biggest single factor in press coverage: having a press release (or press conference) substantially increases chances of pickup because many stories originate directly from releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic is health- or environment-related
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media coverage is often determined more by subject matter than scientific importance. Personal health and climate change consistently get more coverage; health- and environment-related topics attract disproportionate attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published in a high-prestige journal (journal prestige)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-prestige journals drive coverage — six of the top 10 journals in press coverage are health-focused. Examples listed: Nature, Science, Cell, NEJM, Lancet, JAMA. Lower-tier journals get much less pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has practical / societal application (applied research advantage)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public is interested in research with direct practical applications and societal benefits; applied research outperforms basic research in pickup. Emphasize real-world relevance and applications to increase newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains a 'first' or 'record' (novelty/record claims)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases that claim records (first, largest, oldest, most distant) are more likely to be covered — novelty and quantifiable ‘record’ claims are strong hooks for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has compelling visual assets
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals (figures, photos, graphics) increase pickup chances; multimedia makes a release easier to use in coverage and more appealing to editors and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has accessible language
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, non-technical, accessible wording in the press release increases pickup. Language that translates technical findings into plain terms helps journalists and broad audiences understand and reuse the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong narrative angle and clear 'so what?' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong narrative angle; clear 'so what?' framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A press release should present a strong narrative hook and explicitly answer why the finding matters. Framing the research with a clear significance statement or storyline increases news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear human-interest / personal-relatable angle
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that are personal or relatable (human consequences, patient stories, everyday relevance) are more attractive to journalists and audiences than abstract technical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness with the current news cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Is timely with current news cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alignment with ongoing news topics or public debates increases pickup; timing a release when the subject is in the news makes journalists more likely to cover it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of video or interview opportunities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing video assets or the possibility of interviews with researchers (or spokespeople) makes coverage easier and more attractive, aiding pickup and richer reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter-specific biases (fields favored or penalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter effects — some fields get more or less coverage (e.g., personal health and climate change get more; cell biology and applied mathematics get less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage probability varies by discipline; press officers should be aware which fields are typically favored and consider framing strategies to increase appeal for less-covered fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prestige (top universities advantage)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top universities (Harvard, MIT, Stanford) get disproportionate pickup. Institutional brand and reputation influence journalists' attention, so affiliation matters independent of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press office / PIO experience and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: PIO experience matters; press office reputation matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced public information officers and reputable press offices are better at packaging and pitching stories, managing embargoes, and facilitating media access, thereby improving pickup odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo timing alignment with journal publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo timing alignment with journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinating embargoes and timing of release with journal publication affects coverage; alignment with publication schedules and media routines can increase uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthy 'sexy topics' and counter-intuitive findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthy elements: 'Sexy topics' (black holes, exoplanets, cancer cures, AI breakthroughs) and counter-intuitive findings increase coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists favor eye-catching or surprising results. Emphasizing surprising, counter-intuitive, or culturally resonant aspects of research will boost interest.
